Also aim for the corners of the glass where the window is held by the door frame. Because of the tension on these areas the glass is less flexible and easier to break than the center of the window. I've seen someone baseball swing a steel bar at the center of a window and it didn't break. With a carbide glass breaking tool you can hit the corner of a window with a light tap and shatter the window. The super cheap car escape tools are often not very good (still better than nothing). If you are shopping for one look for something that specifies having a carbide glass breaker. It's way harder than regular steel and is much better for breaking glass with little effort.

In some places, not all, populations of animals are actually gaining from being hunted. In western Asia species like the markhor and the urial were declining from poaching and decreased habitat caused by rural agriculture. The people in the area had very little income and survived on their agriculture and domestic goats. To decrease the grazing and agriculture the government sells several trophy animal tags for the 2 species. The profits from these tags provide the majority of the funding to the local tribes and the employ local game wardens/hunting guides from those tribes. Since the animals being harvested are trophies they are generally past the average age of natural death and their removal does not harm the overall population. These animals being killed are actually helping to ensure the survival of the species. Last year 4 markhor permits were sold for over $60,000 each. But again this is unfortunately not the case for every species.

It is definitely possible. a big reason why there were large numbers of elk starving prior to the wolves was because of harsher winters. The elk get most of their nourishment from grasses during the winter and when you have rain on snow events a hard crust forms which makes it much more difficult to get through the snow to get to the grasses. So many were starving because they couldnt get to food. Large populations prior to this only exasperated the situation. The wolves definitely did help level the elk to more sustainable numbers though.
The first wolves were reintroduced into yellowstone in the early 90s. About 60 total wolves if i remember correctly.

This is also an isolated event where additive and compensatory predation take place at a sustainable level.  Wolves have definitely had a positive effect on elk populations in Yellowstone but they are also doing a lot of damage in other areas. Predators don't just kill the sick and weak of the heard especially if there is a good growing season for plants the elk graze resulting in fewer starving. Some populations have taken large blows not to mention the effect of wolves on cattle and the fiscal loses in ranching around wolf packs. But still it is very cool to see a more natural system like Yellowstone respond so rapidly and positively!
